reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Fitzpatrick's Dermatology
clinicalPearls: A form of primary localised cutaneous amyloidosis presenting as intensely itchy, discrete, firm, hyperkeratotic and often hyperpigmented papules
Characteristically involves the shins (pretibial) bilaterally and may also affect the extensor forearms, thighs, and upper back
Papules frequently coalesce into rippled or rough plaques and commonly show the Koebner phenomenon from chronic scratching
The amyloid is keratin-derived, from degenerate keratinocyte (filamentous) material, and is not associated with systemic (AL) amyloidosis
Chronic rubbing and scratching are central, and the condition overlaps with, and may be a variant of, lichen simplex chronicus and prurigo
More common in South-East Asian, Middle-Eastern, and South American populations, with a familial subset associated with OSMR and IL31RA mutations
Diagnosis is confirmed histologically by amyloid in the papillary dermis that stains with Congo red and shows apple-green birefringence under polarised light
Treatment is difficult and centres on breaking the itch-scratch cycle with potent topical corticosteroids (often under occlusion), keratolytics, and phototherapy
reference.pathophysiology: In lichen amyloidosis the amyloid deposits are of keratinocyte origin. Chronic friction and scratching are thought to injure basal keratinocytes, which undergo apoptosis (filamentous degeneration) and shed cytokeratin that is then converted, with the help of dermal cells, into amyloid deposited in the papillary dermis. The keratin-derived nature of the amyloid explains why the disease remains confined to the skin without systemic organ involvement, and the persistence of the itch-scratch cycle continuously supplies degenerate keratin, perpetuating and enlarging the deposits.
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with Congo red staining showing apple-green birefringence and confirming papillary dermal amyloid
Immunohistochemistry for cytokeratin to demonstrate the keratinous origin of the amyloid
Assessment for a family history of primary cutaneous amyloidosis in familial forms
Evaluation to exclude systemic amyloidosis where the presentation is atypical, although this form is not systemic
Documentation of the itch-scratch pattern and Koebnerisation
redFlags: Atypical or widespread deposition prompting exclusion of systemic amyloidosis
Severe intractable pruritus with marked functional or sleep disturbance
Rapidly changing or ulcerating lesions requiring re-biopsy
reference.prognosis: Benign but chronic and often refractory; it poses no systemic threat, but the itch and cosmetic appearance persist and lesions recur while scratching continues.
pitfalls: Assuming an association with systemic amyloidosis, which does not apply to this keratin-derived form
Failing to address the itch-scratch cycle that perpetuates the deposits
Confusing it with lichen simplex chronicus or hypertrophic lichen planus without biopsy
Overlooking familial cases and their inheritance
management: Break the itch-scratch cycle as the mainstay, using potent topical corticosteroids, often under occlusion, together with antipruritic measures
Control pruritus with emollients, menthol preparations, oral antihistamines and, in resistant cases, gabapentinoids
Reduce hyperkeratotic papules and plaques with topical keratolytics, dimethyl sulfoxide or intralesional corticosteroids
Phototherapy with narrowband ultraviolet B or systemic retinoids such as acitretin for extensive or refractory disease
Physical measures and behavioural advice to prevent scratching and Koebnerisation
Reassurance that the condition is skin-limited and not associated with systemic amyloidosis
Consider familial evaluation for OSMR and IL31RA variants where there is a family history
